This 1986 Blue Bird Wanderlodge Still Delivers High-End Motorhome Living Thanks to $110K Renovation
27 photos
Photo: Collecting Cars
Long before today’s luxury motorhomes that feel like rolling homes on wheels, American manufacturers were already crafting some remarkable, opulent recreational vehicles. One of these manufacturers was Blue Bird Corporation, and its most remarkable RV creation was the Wanderlodge, a high-end motorhome aimed at an elite clientele.
When hearing the name Blue Bird, most people think of those iconic yellow school buses, but the US manufacturer has produced a wide variety of other vehicle types, including transit buses, mobile libraries, mobile police command centers, and even motorhomes.
Combining the rugged, durable foundation of a heavy-duty bus with the kind of interior amenities expected in a high-end residence, the Wanderlodge was one of the most luxurious motorhomes of its time, with its pricing comparable with the cost of a medium-sized house.
Initially introduced in 1963 as the Transit Home, this Class A RV was produced by Blue Bird through its Cardinal Manufacturing subsidiary in Fort Valley, Georgia, from 1963 to 2008. It was renamed the Wanderlodge, from mixing the words wanderlust and lodge, in 1968, and it spanned three generations, transitioning from gas-powered front-engine models to powerful rear-engine diesel units, and eventually introducing slide-out expansions in the late 1990s.
Photo: Collecting Cars What’s important to note is that, even though it’s based on Blue Bird’s heavy-duty All American commercial and school bus platform, the Wanderlodge is not a converted school bus . It was envisioned and produced as a luxury Class A recreational vehicle from the get-go, and unlike other mass-produced RVs, it was assembled largely by hand and offered a customizable interior, with over 200 options to choose from for floor plans, cabinetry, appliances, upholstery, and more.
Throughout the 45-year production run, Blue Bird continually refined the motorhome, which was offered in lengths raging from 31 feet (9.4 meters) to 45 feet (13.7 meters). It was widely considered a pioneer and a gold standard in luxury recreational vehicles, and it attracted a select clientele, the likes of Johnny Cash, King Hussein of Jordan, and former U.S. President Jimmy Carter.
An example of the Wanderlodge is now being offered for sale in France, and it perfectly showcases why this classic American motorhome is considered by many better than some modern RVs. What we have here is a 1986 Blue Bird Wanderlodge PT38 that, according to the seller, has benefited from renovations and upgrades worth about $110,000 in recent years.
Photo: Collecting Cars These motorhomes were built with an all-steel chassis to meet school bus safety standards for roll-over protection, and this is reportedly valid for this particular unit as well. Its construction is said to incorporate galvanized steel and aviation-style riveted bodywork, making it way sturdier and more durable than you’d expect a recreational vehicle to be.
Under the hood of this Wanderlodge PT38 unit lies a 12.1-liter Detroit Diesel 8V92 two-stroke turbocharged V8 engine, producing a reported 470 hp. Power is sent to the rear wheels via an Allison four-speed automatic transmission, and the chassis integrates full air-ride suspension, full air brakes, and 22.5-inch chrome alloy wheels fitted with Toyo M170Z tires.
On the outside, it’s finished in a two-tone black and gold color scheme, with gray, red, and black decals, and is adorned with exterior fabric awnings, a full-length roof rack, and a rear access ladder. Several external storage compartments provide plenty of room for luggage and other items, while a slide-out tray holds a grill for outdoor cooking.
Photo: Collecting Cars The interior is where the Wanderlodge’s luxurious nature is more aparent. The living space has a distinct 1980s character due to the color palette dominated by creams, browns, and natural wood tones. The included amenities and choice of materials give it a residential feel, with brown and beige leatherette, beige crushed velvet upholstery, wooden flooring, wooden worktops, and gloss-white and wood veneer-covered cabinets.
The layout provides dedicated spaces for relaxation, cooking, dining, and sleeping, with a seamless flow between areas. Futon sofas at the front are great for socializing and relaxing, a dedicated booth-style dining area provides space for meals and remote work, and the large kitchen lets you cook your favorite meals on the road. There is also a proper double bed at the rear and a bathroom with a shower cabin, a toilet, a washbasin, and storage solutions.
The kitchen is particularly well equipped for a motorhome that’s 40 years old, including an over, a three-burner gas hob, a microwave, and a full-size fridge-freezer. There is also a separate wine and beer refrigerator, along with a toaster and a sink with cold and hot water. According to the listing, the kitchen and plumbing systems have undergone recent renovations.
Other amenities include electrically adjustable front seats, cruise control, a Pioneer double-DIN multimedia system, a television, a Cobra CB radio, and a gas/smoke alarm system.
Photo: Collecting Cars The motorhome is also equipped for self-sufficiency , with a 12kW Kohler generator for powering the onboard amenities. Recently installed lithium batteries with a 560Ah capacity, a Victron charger-converter, and 900 watts of solar panels add to its off-grid capabilities.
Other improvements that have been made lately include a replacement gearbox and rear axle, which were installed in 2014, ten new chassis air cushions, new tires, and a whole body repaint job.
This 1986 Blue Bird Wanderlodge PT38 RV is said to be one of only 63 examples built in this particular length, making it an unusual find, especially on the European market. It was originally registered abroad in 1986 and is now offered for sale out of La Clayette, France, via Collecting Cars.
Before getting carried away by its impressive looks and specification, there are some things worth considering. For instance, the seller notes a hydraulic leak on the lifting jack system, and though the odometer displays just 6,430 miles (10,348 km), the engine hours suggest the motorhome might have actually covered about 202,350 miles (325,650 km).
